title: Network Security & Attacks
summary: Networks are battlegrounds. Learn the attacks — MITM, DDoS, spoofing, hijacking — and the defenses that stop them.

blocks.markdown:
**Network security** is the practice of protecting data in transit and network infrastructure from unauthorized access, disruption, or theft.

- Attackers exploit **protocol weaknesses**, misconfigured devices, or unencrypted traffic.
- Every defense maps to a specific threat — there is no single silver bullet.
- The goal is **confidentiality, integrity, and availability** (CIA) — keep data secret, unaltered, and reachable.
- Understanding attacks is the first step to building defenses.

blocks.subTitle: CIA Triad
blocks.markdown:
The **CIA Triad** is the security framework every network control maps back to.

| Goal | Meaning | Network example |
|---|---|---|
| Confidentiality | Only authorized parties read the data | TLS encryption |
| Integrity | Data is not tampered with in transit | HMAC / digital signatures |
| Availability | Services stay reachable | DDoS mitigation |

An attack always breaks at least one leg of the triad.

- **Passive** attacks (sniffing) observe traffic without changing it.
- **Active** attacks (MITM, DDoS) interfere with or modify traffic.

blocks.subTitle: Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)
blocks.markdown:
A **man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack** is when an attacker secretly positions themselves between two communicating parties, relaying and potentially altering messages without either side knowing.

- The attacker can **read, modify, or inject** data into the stream.
- Common vector: attacker on the same Wi-Fi network intercepts traffic between a user and a website.
- **Defense:** end-to-end encryption ([tls-ssl](tls-ssl)) so the attacker sees only ciphertext they can't read.

blocks.subTitle: Spoofing — IP, ARP, DNS
blocks.markdown:
**Spoofing** means forging an identity to deceive a system or user.

- **IP spoofing** — send packets with a fake source IP to hide the attacker's origin or impersonate a trusted host.
- **ARP spoofing** — broadcast fake ARP replies on a LAN to link the attacker's MAC to a legitimate IP, enabling MITM.
- **DNS spoofing** — return forged DNS answers so victims resolve a domain to the attacker's IP.

**Defenses:** packet filtering (drop spoofed IPs), dynamic ARP inspection, DNSSEC.

blocks.subTitle: DDoS
blocks.markdown:
A **Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS)** attack floods a target with traffic from many machines (a **botnet**) until it can no longer serve legitimate users — an availability attack.

- **Volumetric:** saturate the network link with raw bandwidth (UDP floods).
- **Protocol:** exploit protocol weaknesses (SYN flood exhausts TCP connection state).
- **Application layer:** send expensive HTTP requests (Layer 7 DDoS).

**Defenses:** rate limiting, CDN-based scrubbing, anycast traffic diffusion, ISP-level filtering.

blocks.subTitle: DNS Cache Poisoning
blocks.markdown:
**DNS cache poisoning** injects a false DNS record into a resolver's cache so that all users of that resolver are redirected to the attacker's IP, even though they typed the correct domain.

- Differs from DNS spoofing: poisoning targets the **resolver's cache**, affecting many victims at once.
- Classic attack: guess the transaction ID of a DNS query and race a forged response.
- **Defense:** DNSSEC (cryptographically signs DNS records), randomized source ports, query ID randomization. See [dns](dns).

blocks.subTitle: Packet Sniffing
blocks.markdown:
**Packet sniffing** (passive eavesdropping) is capturing network traffic as it flows across a shared medium — no packets are modified.

- Tools like Wireshark place a NIC in **promiscuous mode** to capture all frames on the segment.
- Dangerous on unencrypted protocols (HTTP, FTP, Telnet) where credentials flow in plaintext.
- **Defense:** encrypt everything (TLS, SSH, VPN) so captured bytes are unreadable ciphertext.

blocks.subTitle: Session Hijacking & Replay
blocks.markdown:
**Session hijacking** steals an authenticated session token to impersonate a logged-in user — the attacker never needs the password.

- Token theft via XSS, sniffing unencrypted cookies, or MITM.

**Replay attacks** record a valid authentication message and re-send it later to gain access.

- **Defense against hijacking:** HTTPS-only cookies (`Secure; HttpOnly`), short token expiry.
- **Defense against replay:** timestamps + nonces (one-time values) so a captured message is invalid when replayed.

blocks.subTitle: Firewalls
blocks.markdown:
A **firewall** filters traffic based on rules — allowing or blocking packets by IP, port, and protocol.

- **Stateless (packet filter):** checks each packet independently against rules.
- **Stateful:** tracks connection state; allows responses to established sessions, blocks unsolicited inbound.
- **Next-gen (NGFW):** inspects application-layer content, user identity, and threat intelligence.

Firewalls define the boundary but don't protect traffic once it's inside. See [nat-firewalls](nat-firewalls).

blocks.subTitle: VPN
blocks.markdown:
A **VPN (Virtual Private Network)** creates an **encrypted tunnel** between a client and a VPN server, routing all traffic through it.

- **What it hides:** your traffic content and source IP from the local network and ISP.
- **What it doesn't hide:** traffic from the VPN server onwards to the destination (the VPN provider sees it instead).
- Protocols: IPsec, OpenVPN, WireGuard.

Used to protect users on untrusted networks (public Wi-Fi) and to securely connect branch offices.

blocks.subTitle: IDS vs IPS
blocks.markdown:
**IDS vs IPS** — detection vs prevention.

| | IDS | IPS |
|---|---|---|
| Role | Detects & alerts on threats | Detects & actively blocks threats |
| Position | Out-of-band (copy of traffic) | Inline (all traffic passes through) |
| Risk | False negatives go unblocked | False positives block legitimate traffic |

- Both use **signature-based** (known patterns) and **anomaly-based** (baseline deviation) detection.
- **IPS is the stricter choice;** misconfigured rules can cause outages.

blocks.subTitle: Encryption & TLS
blocks.markdown:
**Encryption** transforms data so only the holder of the key can read it — the primary tool against eavesdropping and MITM.

- **TLS (Transport Layer Security)** secures HTTP (HTTPS), email, and most modern protocols.
- TLS does three things: **authenticates** the server (certificate), **establishes** a shared key (handshake), **encrypts** the data (symmetric cipher).
- A MITM against TLS requires forging a certificate — blocked by the browser's trusted CA list.

See [tls-ssl](tls-ssl) for the full handshake.

blocks.subTitle: Segmentation & Defense-in-Depth
blocks.markdown:
**Network segmentation** divides a network into zones so a breach in one zone can't freely spread.

- **DMZ:** servers reachable from the internet sit in an isolated zone; internal systems are behind a second firewall.
- **VLANs** segment at Layer 2 within a data center.

**Defense-in-depth** stacks multiple independent controls (firewall + IPS + TLS + segmentation) so that defeating one layer doesn't expose everything. No single control is trusted to be perfect.

Common mistakes:

- **"A firewall is enough."** Firewalls block at the perimeter; threats inside the network (insider attack, lateral movement) bypass them entirely.
- **"VPN = anonymity."** VPN shifts trust to the provider; it's not encryption for the whole internet.
- **"HTTPS means the site is safe."** TLS only encrypts the channel — the server behind it can still be malicious or compromised.
- **"IDS will catch everything."** Signature-based IDS misses novel (zero-day) attacks.

blocks.subTitle: What is MITM and how do you prevent it?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a man-in-the-middle attack and how do you prevent it?**

An attacker secretly relays communication between two parties, able to read or modify data. Prevention: use end-to-end TLS (so the attacker sees ciphertext), validate certificates (rejects forged ones), use HSTS (forces HTTPS, blocks downgrades), and avoid unencrypted protocols.

blocks.subTitle: How does a VPN protect you?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How does a VPN protect you and what are its limits?**

A VPN encrypts all traffic from your device to the VPN server, hiding content and your real IP from the local network and ISP. Limit: traffic from the VPN server to the final destination is not protected by the VPN — the provider can see it. Also, VPNs don't protect against phishing or malware on the endpoint.

blocks.subTitle: IDS vs IPS
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?**

An **IDS** (Intrusion Detection System) monitors a copy of traffic and alerts on suspicious patterns — it cannot block. An **IPS** (Intrusion Prevention System) sits inline and can actively drop or modify malicious packets. The IPS is stronger but carries the risk that a bad rule blocks legitimate traffic.

blocks.subTitle: What is DNS cache poisoning?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is DNS cache poisoning and how is it mitigated?**

An attacker injects a fake DNS record into a resolver's cache, redirecting all users of that resolver to a malicious IP. Mitigation: DNSSEC (signs records cryptographically so forged answers are rejected), randomized query IDs and source ports (make guessing the transaction ID infeasible).

blocks.subTitle: How do you mitigate DDoS?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you mitigate a DDoS attack?**

Layered approach: rate limiting at the edge (drop traffic above threshold), CDN/anycast scrubbing centers absorb volumetric floods, ISP-level BGP blackholing for extreme events, SYN cookies to handle SYN floods without exhausting state. For L7 DDoS: challenge-response (CAPTCHA), WAF rules to block abusive request patterns.

blocks.subTitle: Defense-in-depth explained
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is defense-in-depth?**

Defense-in-depth is the strategy of layering multiple independent security controls so that defeating one does not compromise the whole system. Example: a packet reaches a web server only after passing through a firewall, IPS, TLS termination, and WAF. Each layer assumes the previous one might fail. Borrowed from military thinking — concentric rings of defense.
